newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Big power rows could prick Asian bubble - Ramos.
newsitem.headline: Big power rows could prick Asian bubble - Ramos.

text.p: Big-power conflicts could "burst the bubble of stability" in the Asia-Pacific region and wreck APEC's potential as the world's biggest free-trade area, Philippine President Fidel Ramos said on Monday.

Ramos said uncertainties over China's intentions in the South China Sea, enmities on the Korean peninsula, the future of the U.S.-Japanese defence alliance and the evolution of a new Russia from the ruins of communism worried small Asian nations.
"The regional environment continues to be unsettled because the big powers have yet to clear up their interests and intentions," he said.

Leaders of the 18-member economies of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum, which includes the United States, Japan and China, agreed at a summit held in the Philippines last week to step up the creation of a free-trade area encompassing half the world's wealth.
Ramos, speaking at a seminar on Southeast Asian security and the role of external powers in regional peace, said security concerns remained high on the agenda of Southeast Asian nations.

"If APEC is to realise its potentials, our countries must first of all keep the peace among themselves. Any explosion of violence (involving the big powers) in any part of the Asia-Pacific will burst the bubble of stability that keeps its 'economic miracle' going," he said.
Even if the military balance among the big powers held, greed arising from unrestrained economic competition could ruin Asia's inter-connected markets, he said.
He urged the "middle powers" to exercise their "moral persuasion" to help keep regional peace.
He specifically referred to Australia, New Zealand and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), which groups Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, the Philippines, Singapore, Brunei and Vietnam.

Citing the Malay proverb: "When elephants fight, the mousedeer between them is killed", Ramos said: "The ASEAN states have shown they need not be passive spectators -- hapless mousedeers -- in the interplay among the great powers in the region.
"Now, for the first time in its history, Southeast Asia is becoming a power in the world -- and in its own right."
Ramos referred to what he called the "anomaly and anachronism ... (of) Japan remaining a strategic client of the United States."

"This can only fan an unhealthy kind of nationalism in a nation acutely aware of its political uniqueness and economic power, increasing the danger that the bitter disputes over trade between the two countries would spill over into their security relationship."
He added: "How China exercises its economic, political and military power must also concern us all -- and none more so than we Southeast Asians, who are its closest neighbours.

"China's rapidly expanding economy will unavoidably generate political and military pressures on the Asia-Pacific, even assuming that Beijing made no effort to build its capability to project power beyond its borders."
Ramos said China's integration into the Asia-Pacific community was necessary "if we are to have enduring regional stability".

Ramos said the success of the APEC summit and the visit to Manila last week of Chinese President Jiang Zemin should reinforce ASEAN optimism that a solution could be found to the dispute over the South China Sea's Spratly islands.
The potentially oil-rich reefs are claimed wholly or in part by China, Taiwan, Vietnam, the Philippines, Malaysia and Brunei.
